target: वह हर दिन बिना नागा स्कूल जाती है।
english: She goes to school every day without fail.
tip: The verb marks the subject's gender too: वह जाती है (vah jaati hai = she goes) has -ती because she's female; a boy would be जाता है (jaata hai).

target: मैं हर शाम हेडफ़ोन लगाकर संगीत सुनता हूँ।
english: I listen to music with headphones every evening.
tip: 'Wear' depends on the item: हेडफ़ोन लगाकर (headphone lagaakar) uses लगाना (lagaana = attach); clothes take पहनना (pahenna). Each item picks its verb.

target: मैं रोज़ सुबह ठीक छह बजे उठता हूँ।
english: I wake up every morning at exactly six o'clock.
tip: ठीक (theek) usually means 'fine, okay' – but before a time it means sharp: ठीक छह बजे (theek chhah baje) = at exactly six.

target: मेरे दादाजी सुबह-सवेरे टहलने जाते हैं।
english: My grandfather goes for a walk early in the morning.
tip: Going somewhere to do something uses the -ने (-ne) verb form: टहलने जाते हैं (tahalne jaate hain) = go for a stroll, literally 'go to stroll'. No 'for' needed.

target: क्या वह सुबह उठकर सबसे पहले अख़बार पढ़ता है?
english: Does he read the newspaper first thing after waking up?
tip: Hindi has no '-est'. सबसे पहले (sabse pehle) = first of all, literally 'than all, earlier'. सबसे (sabse) + any quality word means 'the most'.

target: वे लोग हर रोज़ बस से दफ़्तर जाते हैं।
english: Those people go to the office by bus every day.
tip: से (se) means 'from' – and also 'by': बस से (bas se) = by bus. Every means of transport takes से; context tells you which sense is meant.

target: सीता योग और ध्यान दोनों हर सुबह करती है।
english: Sita does both yoga and meditation every morning.
tip: In an 'X और Y' list, दोनों (donon = both) comes at the end: योग और ध्यान दोनों (yog aur dhyaan donon) = both yoga and meditation.

target: मेरा छोटा भाई हमेशा सबको हँसाता रहता है।
english: My little brother always makes everyone laugh.
tip: One vowel makes it 'make someone laugh': हँसना (hansna = laugh) → हँसाता (hansaata = makes laugh). No extra 'make' verb – the -आ- (-aa-) does it.

target: क्या तुम्हें अलग-अलग तरह का खाना बनाना आता है?
english: Can you cook different types of food?
tip: Skills 'come to you': खाना बनाना आता है (khaana banaana aata hai) = literally 'does making food come to you'. Knowing how = the skill + आना (aana = come).

target: बच्चे गर्मी की लंबी छुट्टी में ननिहाल जाते हैं।
english: Children go to their maternal grandparents' home during long summer holidays.
tip: ननिहाल (nanihaal) is one word for 'mother's parents' home' – a classic summer-holiday destination. Hindi has exact words for each side of the family.

target: क्या तुम्हारी बिल्ली दिन भर इधर-उधर घूमती रहती है?
english: Does your cat wander around all day?
tip: रहती (rahti) after another verb means 'keeps on': घूमती रहती है (ghoomti rahti hai) = keeps wandering. रहना (rahna = stay) makes an action ongoing.

target: मैं हर रात ठीक दस बजे बिस्तर पर सो जाता हूँ।
english: I go to bed at exactly ten o'clock every night.
tip: सो जाता हूँ (so jaata hoon) = literally 'I go off to sleep'. Adding जाना (jaana = go) marks the change as complete – सोना (sona) alone is just 'sleep'.

target: मैं खाना खाने के तुरंत बाद साबुन से हाथ धोता हूँ।
english: I wash my hands with soap immediately after eating.
tip: 'After' comes after: खाने के तुरंत बाद (khaane ke turant baad) = literally 'of eating immediately after'. Time words like बाद (baad) follow their noun.

target: हमारे पड़ोसी एक-दूसरे के सुख-दुख में साथ देते हैं।
english: Our neighbors stand by each other in good times and bad.
tip: However long the sentence, the verb normally comes last: time, place and object all pile up before साथ देते हैं (saath dete hain = stand by), which waits at the end.

target: मैं महीने में कम से कम दो बार दोस्तों से मिलता हूँ।
english: I meet friends at least twice a month.
tip: कम से कम (kam se kam) = at least, literally 'less than less'. Hindi builds it by comparing कम (kam = less) with itself.

target: यह ट्रेन रोज़ देर से आती है।
english: This train comes late every day.
tip: देर से आती है (der se aati hai) = comes late, literally 'comes with delay'. देर (der) is a noun – Hindi says 'with delay' where English says 'late'.

target: आज सब्ज़ी मंडी बंद है।
english: The vegetable market is closed today.
tip: Hindi has no 'the' or 'a' – सब्ज़ी मंडी बंद है (sabzi mandi band hai) is just 'vegetable market closed is'. Context alone tells you which market.

target: गर्म कपड़े सर्दियों में ज़रूरी होते हैं।
english: Warm clothes are necessary in winter.
tip: होते हैं (hote hain) marks a general truth: ज़रूरी होते हैं (zaroori hote hain = are, as a rule, necessary). Plain हैं (hain) would pin it to right now.

target: आज सुबह से ही बारिश हो रही है।
english: It has been raining since this morning.
tip: English says 'has been raining'; Hindi keeps plain 'is raining': बारिश हो रही है (baarish ho rahi hai = rain is happening) + सुबह से (subah se = since morning).

target: क्या यह सच है कि तुम जा रहे हो?
english: Is it true that you are leaving?
tip: क्या (kya) up front is a spoken question mark: क्या यह सच है (kya yeh sach hai) = is this true? Without it, यह सच है (yeh sach hai) states 'this is true'.

target: छोटे कमरे में ज़्यादा सामान नहीं आता।
english: Not much stuff fits in a small room.
tip: Things 'come into' a space when they fit: ज़्यादा सामान नहीं आता (zyaada saamaan nahin aata = more stuff doesn't come) = no more fits. Rooms, boxes, clothes all work this way.

target: क्या तुम सुबह उठकर दूध पीते हो?
english: Do you drink milk after waking up in the morning?
tip: -कर (-kar) glued to a verb means 'after doing it': उठकर (uthkar = having gotten up). One ending does the work of English 'after waking up'.

target: यह दवाई बुखार के लिए है।
english: This medicine is for fever.
tip: के लिए (ke liye = for) comes after its noun, not before: बुखार के लिए (bukhaar ke liye = fever for). Hindi's little linking words all trail the noun.

target: मुझे एक ज़रूरी फ़ोन करना है।
english: I have to make an important phone call.
tip: मुझे ... करना है (mujhe ... karna hai) is literally 'to me it is to-do' – Hindi's 'I have to'. फ़ोन करना है (phone karna hai) = I have to make a call.

target: मुझे हर तरह की किताबें पढ़ना बेहद पसंद है।
english: I absolutely love reading all kinds of books.
tip: Liking lands on you in Hindi – मुझे पसंद है (mujhe pasand hai) is literally 'to me it is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे, never मैं.

target: ग्वाले ने ताज़ा दूध बर्तन में डाला।
english: The milkman poured fresh milk in the vessel.
tip: In past tense for action verbs, add ने (ne) after the subject. मैंने खाना खाया (mainne khaana khaaya = I ate food). The verb then agrees with the object, not the subject.

target: आज का मौसम बिलकुल भी अच्छा नहीं है।
english: Today's weather is not good at all.
tip: भी (bhi) normally means 'also', but next to नहीं (nahin) it means 'at all': बिलकुल भी अच्छा नहीं (bilkul bhi achha nahin) = not good at all.

target: मेरे फ़ोन की बैटरी ख़त्म हो गई है।
english: My phone's battery is dead.
tip: The battery 'became finished': ख़त्म हो गई है (khatm ho gayi hai). Hindi frames new states as becoming – phones die, tanks fill, trains run late by 'becoming'.

target: मेरा बचपन इस छोटे से गाँव में बीता था।
english: I spent my childhood in this small village.
tip: You don't spend a childhood in Hindi – it passes on its own: बीता था (beeta tha = passed). बचपन (bachpan = childhood) is the subject; the village is just where it happened.

target: क्या तुम्हें इस नए शहर में रहना अच्छा लगता है?
english: Do you like living in this new city?
tip: Liking lands on you: तुम्हें (tumhein = to you) plus अच्छा लगता है (achha lagta hai = strikes as good) = you like it. The person liking is the target, not the doer.
